toc.title: Can safety anchors alone get you there?
Co-regulation matters, even when you're not talking about your stuff
Your history gives you a leg up, or it doesn't
Where to start if you're on the harder end

blocks.p: Do you think anybody and everybody can recover from a stuck, traumatized state simply by accessing more of their Polyvagal safety state? The annoying, short answer is that it depends. I know. I can't stand when people say that either, but that is the answer. It's both yes and no.
Context really matters, and so does co-regulation. So does your history of healthy attachments. And there are obstacles to self-regulation, even when you're finding success with it.

blocks.h: Can safety anchors alone get you there?

blocks.p: Here's the question as someone in my community asked it: could everyone access enough safety through safety anchors alone to move on to the next step, which is directly experiencing what we have inside of us?

I don't want to say everyone. I don't like talking in huge generalities like "yes, my system works for everybody." That feels irresponsible to me. If you're already on the path of recovery and self-regulation, I generally think, yeah. Can I promise it? No, of course not.

But everyone? No, I don't think so. If you're living alone, or you're truly in danger, practicing this stuff is fine, but you probably need another layer of literal safety in your environment: literal safety, and safe enough people in your life. Then practicing on top of that is generally helpful. So it depends on context. I don't think just anyone, in whatever their current context is, can stumble onto this material and be set, even though I wrote it for a very general audience.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: Co-regulation matters, even when you're not talking about your stuff

blocks.p: Co-regulation is important, even if it's not specifically about disclosing past stuff or how you're functioning now. Just having co-regulation in your life, predictable safety, is kind of necessary. Can we move on to directly experiencing what's inside us if we don't have good enough co-regulation in our life? That's the real question.
Is it possible to do this stuff truly alone? Probably not. Alone in an environment where you're captive and in literal danger? No, probably not.

But alone in the sense that you go to work and chit chat with people, but you don't feel super connected and fulfilled, and then you go home and you're mostly alone, or you have a pet? I think you can do a lot of good with just that. It'll probably be a lot harder.

If you're surrounded by true friends, maybe a spouse or partner, pets, a yoga studio where you go and feel connection and can move around, a therapist: if you start stacking these pieces up, your potential to get unstuck, and to benefit from all of these things, is probably a lot higher.

blocks.h: Your history gives you a leg up, or it doesn't

blocks.p: Your history of attachment, your history of healthy co-regulation growing up, which leads to self-regulation: that's a big part of this. It gives you a leg up.
Deb Dana said it well on the podcast:

q: When we have enough co-regulation it builds the platform for us to be able to use self-regulation.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana: Book 2 and COVID-19 (episode 54)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/98a53db3-770b-483d-ad74-40256d4c6b3a)

blocks.p: So someone who's alone and doesn't have the best co-regulation, maybe even a little below good enough, can still be on the path. They can go on Instagram and YouTube. They can read books. But they're way, way behind compared to someone who's in therapy and doing yoga and meditations and retreats.

blocks.h: Where to start if you're on the harder end

blocks.p: Could that person, on the more extreme end of the spectrum, still start somewhere? I think so.

ul: Can they set up their home environment to feel a little more safe? I think so.
Can they listen to what's happening within them? I think so.
Movement might be too much for them, I don't know. But they can maybe use music, or their sensory inputs.

blocks.p: They might be able to start doing little things that open up more capacity for the next step, or for a connection with a new pet, or a community, or something. But it's probably going to be a longer process.
On the extreme end, if you're not in a literally safe environment, that's the thing to address first. Beyond that, there are barriers that can get in the way for anybody:

ol: Behavioral adaptations. That's true for anybody. How far you are down the road to self-regulation, the intensity and frequency of those behaviors, and your ability to sit with them and feel the emotion underneath all shape your potential to navigate through them.
Cognitive adaptations. The things we tell ourselves that keep us stuck.

What happens when you do have some success. When you feel a bit more safety, all of a sudden you're crying, or flight activation kicks in. That's a good sign, but for someone who's not prepared for it, it can become a barrier.

The people around you. Someone in my community added this one, and I love it. When you start to improve, it affects the people around you, and they might have a reaction to the change in you. I look at the person I'm working with as a gear in a machine. When that gear starts turning differently, the other gears either have to get out of the machine or start churning along with it. And the first thing they're going to do is resist it.
